texts.label: A
texts.title: Oakwood Primary School — after-school homework club

paragraphs.text: Oakwood Primary School — after-school homework club. The homework club runs in the school library from 3.15 pm to 4.45 pm on Mondays, Tuesdays and Thursdays during term time. It is open to pupils in Years 3 to 6, and up to twenty-five children can attend each session. Two teaching assistants supervise the club, help children to understand their tasks and make sure that everyone has somewhere quiet to work.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The club costs £3 a session, payable through the school payment system by the Friday before each week; children who receive free school meals may attend without charge. A drink and a piece of fruit are provided at the start of each session, but children should not bring sweets or crisps. Laptops are available for homework that needs the internet, and children may use them only for school work.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Children must be collected from the main gate by 4.45 pm. If someone other than a parent will be collecting, please tell the school office in writing beforehand. Children in Year 6 may walk home alone if a parent has signed the permission form. Places are allocated for a whole term, and parents who wish to cancel should give two weeks’ notice.
paragraphs.label: C

texts.label: B
texts.title: Moving house? Four removal services compared

paragraphs.text: Swift Movers. A family business with twenty years’ experience of local moves. Prices are based on the number of rooms and include packing materials, although packing itself is extra. Two staff and one van are sent for most jobs, so moves from larger homes may take two days. Free quotes are given after a home visit.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: City Van and Man. The cheapest option for small moves such as students or single rooms. You pay by the hour, with a minimum of two hours, and you are expected to help carry items. No packing service is offered, and fragile items are carried at the customer’s own risk.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Premier Relocations. A full service, including packing, dismantling and reassembling furniture, and unpacking at the new home. Every move is covered by insurance up to £50,000. Prices are higher than those of most local firms, but a fixed price is agreed in advance, so customers pay no more if the job takes longer than planned.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Green Crate Moves. Instead of cardboard boxes, customers are given strong plastic crates, which are delivered a week before the move and collected a week afterwards. The company uses electric vans for moves within the city and offsets emissions on longer journeys. Weekend moves cost 20 per cent more than weekday ones.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Joining the staff mentoring scheme. The mentoring scheme pairs employees who would like guidance on their career with more experienced colleagues from a different department. It is open to all permanent staff who have completed their probation period, and there is no charge to take part. Applications open twice a year, in January and July, and pairs are matched by the learning team within four weeks of the closing date. Staff on fixed-term contracts of more than a year may also apply, and you can apply as a mentee only once every two years.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Mentors are volunteers with at least five years’ experience in the company. They receive a half-day training session before they start and are not expected to be experts in the mentee’s field; their role is to listen, ask questions and share what they have learned, not to solve problems on the mentee’s behalf. Mentors may support no more than two mentees at any one time. Anyone interested in becoming a mentor should speak to the learning team, who hold an information session for new mentors each spring.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Pairs agree how and when they will meet, but most meet for about an hour once a month, either in person or by video call. Meetings should take place during working hours, and line managers are asked to allow the time. What is discussed is confidential and is not reported to the mentee’s manager unless the mentee asks for this. Pairs are encouraged to set one or two goals at their first meeting and to review them regularly.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Each partnership lasts for twelve months. Halfway through, both mentor and mentee are asked to complete a short online review, which helps the learning team improve the scheme. Either person may end the arrangement early by informing the learning team, who will offer the mentee a new mentor if they would like one. At the end of the year, mentees receive a certificate of participation.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Time off for public duties. The company supports employees who carry out public duties outside their normal job, such as serving on a jury, acting as a school governor or volunteering as a special constable. This policy explains how much time off you can take and whether you will be paid for it. Any request should be made to your line manager as early as possible, with a copy of the letter or document that confirms the duty. Public duties do not include political activity, such as campaigning for an election.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: If you are called for jury service, you will receive your normal pay for up to ten working days. The court pays an allowance for loss of earnings, and you must claim this and pass it to the payroll team, who will deduct it from your salary. If your jury service lasts longer than ten days, the company will continue to pay you only the difference between the court allowance and your normal pay.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: For other public duties, you may take up to six days of paid leave a year. Time needed beyond this may be taken as unpaid leave or as part of your annual holiday, by agreement with your manager. Managers may refuse or postpone a request only if the absence would cause serious difficulties for the team, and they must explain the reason in writing. Unpaid leave does not affect your pension or holiday entitlement.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Employees who are asked to give evidence as a witness in court are entitled to paid leave for the time needed, however long it takes, and this does not count towards the six-day limit. If you are unsure whether an activity counts as a public duty, contact the human resources team before making plans. A record of all time taken for public duties is kept by human resources, and your manager may ask to see the relevant paperwork afterwards.
paragraphs.label: D

texts.label: E
texts.title: The return of the spoken book

paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, a recorded book was a specialised product. It was made mainly for people who could not read print, sold on sets of records or cassettes that were heavy, expensive and easily damaged, and it occupied a small corner of the publishing world that most readers never visited. In the past two decades that situation has changed completely. Audiobooks are now one of the fastest-growing parts of the book trade in many countries, and a large share of new titles is released in spoken form on the same day as in print. The transformation happened with little planning, and it has surprised many people who work in publishing.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The change owes most to technology. A book that once filled a shelf of cassettes now occupies a small file on a phone, can be downloaded in seconds and resumes automatically at the point where the listener stopped. Subscription services have reduced the price of each title, and the growth of long commutes, podcasts and wireless headphones has created a generation of people used to listening while they do something else. Publishers who once recorded only their bestsellers now record a large part of their lists. The number of people who report having listened to at least one audiobook in the past year has roughly doubled in several markets within a decade.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The way audiobooks are made has changed too. Early recordings were often abridged, with long passages cut to reduce the number of tapes, and many were read by a single actor with little direction. Today almost all titles are recorded unabridged, and publishers spend considerable effort choosing narrators, sometimes casting several voices for a single novel. Many authors now record their own non-fiction, on the assumption that listeners want to hear the writer’s voice, although authors are not always the most skilled readers of their own work. A well-chosen narrator can make a modest book a success, and a poor one can damage the reputation of a good one. Some productions now include music and sound effects, closer to radio drama than to a simple reading.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: A question that has attracted researchers is whether listening to a book is really the same as reading it. Studies that tested comprehension after people read or listened to the same passage have generally found little difference for straightforward narrative texts. For complex material, however, readers tend to do better, apparently because they can slow down, reread difficult sentences and look back at earlier sections, which listeners do far less often even when the technology allows it. Listening while doing another demanding task reduces understanding considerably. Some researchers suggest that listeners should treat difficult audiobooks more like lectures, pausing to think rather than letting the recording run.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Some critics have argued that listening is a lesser form of reading, a way of consuming books without the effort that makes them worthwhile. Defenders point out that for most of human history stories were heard rather than read, that reading aloud was the normal way of sharing books in many households until the twentieth century, and that listening demands its own kind of attention. For people with visual impairments or reading difficulties, the question of which form is superior has never been a relevant one. In some cultures, oral storytelling remains more highly valued than written literature.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: There is evidence that audiobooks bring new people to books rather than simply replacing print. Surveys of listeners in several countries have found that a substantial proportion also read printed books and that many say they now consume more books in total than before. A smaller but significant group consists of people who rarely read print at all, including many who describe themselves as too busy to sit down with a book. For publishers, this suggests that the spoken book has widened the market rather than dividing it. Children who listen to stories read aloud also tend to develop larger vocabularies, a finding that has encouraged many schools to use audiobooks in lessons.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The growth has brought new tensions. Narrators, many of whom are actors, have raised concerns about pay and about the use of synthetic voices produced by computer, which some services have begun to offer for lower-selling titles. Libraries, which lend a great many audiobooks, have complained about licensing terms that make digital copies much more expensive for them than for individual buyers. These disputes are unlikely to be settled quickly, since they involve questions about ownership and value that the book trade is still working out. Authors, too, have questioned whether they receive a fair share of income from subscription services.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: What seems clear is that the spoken book is no longer a substitute for the real thing but a form in its own right, with its own skills, its own audience and its own economics. The oldest way of sharing stories has returned through the newest technology, and for many people the choice between reading and listening now depends less on principle than on whether their hands and eyes are free. Listening, in the end, is simply another way of reading.
paragraphs.label: H
